record.canonical_text: The office is making room for an old idea: a desk that belongs to you. In some workplaces, assigned desks are returning. Companies are reducing their reliance on hot-desking, a system in which workers are not given a personal desk and use whichever desk is free. Scotiabank and iCapital Network are among the companies connected to this quiet shift, according to reporting from Bisnow's New York Office Conference. The change comes as employees express dissatisfaction with hot-desking. Korn Ferry points to several concerns. The office may compare poorly with a home workspace. Workers may sit close to unfamiliar colleagues. The daily work setting may also feel less predictable and less consistent.

record.canonical_text: One reason the desk matters may be psychological, not practical. In Gensler data reported by Bisnow, 87% of workers with assigned desks reported a sense of belonging at work, compared with 74% of workers without assigned desks. The gap in reported ability to concentrate was also clear: 80% versus 67%. These figures show an association, not proof that assigned desks caused the difference.

record.canonical_text: ## Main Story Walk into some offices today, and one old idea is quietly returning: the assigned desk. An assigned desk is kept for one worker. It is different from hot-desking. In a hot-desking office, workers do not have a fixed desk. They choose an empty desk when they arrive. Hot-desking became more common than before the pandemic. It allowed companies to use desks as shared space. But some workers have not been happy with the system. They want a work area that feels more stable and predictable.

This shows a connection, not proof that the desk caused the difference.

record.canonical_text: The result was clear for fruit and vegetables. After 3 months, sales rose by 1.71 standard deviations. In everyday terms, that was about 6,170 portions more per store each week. After 6 months, the increase was 2.42 standard deviations, or about 9,820 more portions each week. Sweets moved in the other direction. After 3 months, sales fell by 1.05 standard deviations. That was about 1,359 fewer portions per store each week. However, total store sales did not change in a statistically significant way. A related survey included 150 women aged 18 to 45. Fruit and vegetable buying increased in households using the changed stores, while it fell in comparison households. Sweets buying did not show a significant effect.

record.canonical_text: A café is no longer only a place for coffee and conversation. For some people, it is also a place to work for hours with a laptop. These customer-workers buy something, take a seat, and use a public space for work-related tasks. For café owners, this creates a difficult choice. Should they welcome this customer group, or protect the space for shorter visits and social use? 2 recent sources show that both answers are now being tested. A 2021 qualitative study by L. Mimoun and A. Gruen, published in the *Journal of Service Research*, examined this question. In London, it covered 38 third places. Researchers made 52 observation visits, interviewed 27 customers and 12 service providers, and reviewed 55 media sources. The study places these businesses into 4 groups. Archetypal places discourage work. Status Quo places do not clearly choose between workers and social customers, and this is where conflict is described as strongest. Compromise places try to serve both groups but may struggle to enforce their rules. Productive Third Places, or PTPs, clearly target customer-workers and adapt the space for them.

For café owners, this creates a difficult choice: should they welcome this customer group or protect the space for shorter visits and social use? Two recent sources show that both answers are now being tested. A 2021 qualitative study by L. Mimuun and A. Groon, published in the Journal of Service Research, examined this question. In London, it covered 38 third places. Researchers made 52 observation visits, interviewed 27 customers and 12 service providers, and reviewed 55 media sources. The study places these businesses into four groups. Archetypal places discourage work. Status quo places do not clearly choose between workers and social customers, and this is where conflict is described as strongest. Compromise places try to serve both groups, but may struggle to enforce their rules. Productive third places, or PTPs, clearly target customer-workers and adapt the space for them.

record.canonical_text: At an airport gate, a line can start before anyone asks for one. The passenger's boarding group has not been called, yet people gather near the gate and prepare to board. Flight attendants have a name for this behavior: gate lice. The behavior may look wasteful. But psychologists do not describe it as simply irrational. Psychologist Stephen Reicher explains it as a response to uneven risks. If a passenger delays joining the line, there may be a small chance of missing a connecting flight. If they stand early, the cost is much smaller: a few unnecessary minutes of waiting. That calculation can turn a quiet gate area into a crowded one. Standing in line feels like a way to stay ready, even when the boarding group has not been called.

record.canonical_text: ## Main Story At a café or restaurant, the bill may end with a question: how much would you like to tip? A screen often shows a few suggested percentages and asks you to pick one. The word recommended sounds helpful. But it can also become the first number in your mind. Before you decide what the service was worth, the screen may have already set a starting point. A 2014 study looked closely at this idea using more than 13 million credit card transactions in New York City taxis. Around a $15 fare, the recommended tip menu changed suddenly. The researchers used this change in a regression discontinuity design.

record.canonical_text: A phone does not need to light up in your hand to change a task. A sound may be enough. In another study, even a silent phone on a desk was linked to lower attention. A study by Upshaw, Stevens, Ganis, and Zabelina tested 73 college students. They worked through a letter task for 960 trials. In some trials, they heard a notification sound. In others, they heard a neutral sound. They did not look at or touch a phone. The result was clear: responses were slower during trials with notification sounds. Brain recordings also showed a larger signal after those sounds. This happened even though the students kept working and did not check a screen.

record.canonical_text: A second study by Skowronek, Seifert, and Lindberg tested 42 university students. Their phones were powered off, and no notifications arrived. The researchers compared a phone on the desk with a phone in another room. Performance was lower when the phone stayed on the desk. The attention score averaged about 100 on the desk, compared with about 109 when the phone was away. Processing speed showed the same pattern: it was lower when the phone stayed on the desk. Together, these studies show 2 different moments. A notification can affect a person during a task. A phone can also be linked to lower performance without making a sound.

record.canonical_text: Reach is the second story. Amazon reports 600 million active Alexa endpoints and says tens of millions joined Alexa Plus Early Access before U.S. availability. Endpoints is Amazon's term, not a count of unique people. Google says Android Auto supports over 250 million cars, while Gemini for Home targets devices made during the previous decade. These reports point to a strategy: add software to places people already use, not a replacement phone.

record.canonical_text: The most important question in the new space-security story is not simply whether satellites can be attacked. It is this: Is the weapon itself in orbit? On September 14, 2026, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit. He said they were meant to protect U.S. forces from hostile actions. An official U.S. Space Force article published the next day described this as the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had put weapons in orbit.

record.canonical_text: The same pattern appeared in 2026. Small pouches appeared at Prada, Loewe, Miu Miu, and Valentino. At the same time, very large bags appeared at Celine, Altuzarra, Toteme, Stella McCartney, and Kallmeyer. Some Fall/Winter 2026 shoulder bags from Chanel, Miu Miu, and Bottega Veneta were even large enough for a laptop. Mini bags also received strong attention from fashion editors. One fashion magazine called them a major Fall 2026 styling direction. But another offered a more mixed view, saying that autumn was bringing back larger bags while still keeping smaller clutches and top-handle bags in the picture. One trend company also reported a 152% rise in retail adoption for oversized clutches in 2026. That is a company estimate, but it adds an important counterpoint. The clearest answer is this: tiny bags are gaining attention in some fashion spaces, but they are not winning everywhere. Small and large bags are appearing side by side.

record.canonical_text: ## Main Story A lemon tart with chopped pickles sounds like a joke—or at least a strange snack. But Lawson says an AI program suggested the pairing, and it became the starting point for a real convenience-store product. The idea did not stay on a computer screen. Human product specialists made samples, tasted them, and adjusted the taste and appearance. Lawson then planned a sale of the finished product.

Then he remembered those warm fingers around his hand.

record.canonical_text:
A small slider inside your refrigerator may look unimportant.

“Low” on one side. “High” on the other.

But this simple control can help fresh food last longer.

Many crisper drawers offer low-humidity and high-humidity settings. Some refrigerators have two separate drawers. Others let users change the setting with a slider.

The key is not simply, “Fruit goes here, and vegetables go there.”

The real question is:

“Does this food release a lot of ethylene gas, or does it quickly lose water and wilt?”

Low-humidity drawers allow more air to move through. This matters because fruits release ethylene as they ripen. If nearby produce stays exposed to the gas, it may ripen too quickly and spoil.

record.canonical_text:
A parent’s life can change.

They may grow up in a family with low social status. Later, they may move into a higher social position.

But does this move also change how they raise their own children?

A 2026 study in *Child Development* looked at this question. It was part of the Dunedin Study, which has followed people born in New Zealand from April 1972 to March 1973.

The parenting study included 719 parent-child pairs. This was 95% of the people who could take part. The parents were 32.7 years old on average. Their children were 3.4 years old on average.

Researchers used job status to compare each parent’s childhood and adult life. They made four groups: parents who stayed low, moved up, stayed high, or moved down.

Then they studied two parts of parenting.

One was sensitive parenting. This means noticing a child’s needs and responding in a warm, positive way.

record.canonical_text:
The other was cognitive stimulation. This means helping a child think, explore, and learn.

Parents who moved up showed better parenting in both areas than parents who stayed in the low group.

However, they did not reach the level of parents who stayed in the high group.

In other words, they were in the middle.

Researchers then looked at the parents’ own childhood experiences. After they included the parenting that adults had received as children, the differences became 13% to 15% smaller. Some differences still remained.

Childhood thinking ability and self-control explained more. These factors reduced the gap with the stable-low group by about 30%. They reduced the gap with the stable-high group by about 50%.

After this step, the difference from the stable-high group was no longer statistically clear for either type of parenting. But the upward group still remained above the stable-low group.

record.canonical_text:
A quiet question at home may become an important research question:

What happens when a young child often has conflict with a parent?

A 2026 study looked at this question through family relationships, screen time, and children’s behavior.

The study followed children aged 3 to 6 in Fuyang, Anhui, China. The final analysis included 532 children. Their mothers answered questions about the children and their family relationships.

The researchers collected information three times. Each check was four months apart.

They asked about two parts of the parent-child relationship: closeness and conflict. They also asked about the children’s daily screen time and behavior problems.

The main result was clear in its direction.

For preschool children, screen time is only one part of daily life. A 2026 study published in *Frontiers in Psychology* asks whether it is also connected with the relationship between children and their mothers.

The study followed children aged 3 to 6 in Fuyang, Anhui, China. It used three surveys, with four months between each one. The first survey included 619 children. The final analysis included 532 children, with mothers answering the questionnaires.

The researchers measured two sides of the parent-child relationship: closeness and conflict. They also measured each child’s average daily screen time.

record.canonical_text:
Finally, they looked at two types of behavior problems. One type involves difficulties turned inward, such as emotional and peer problems. The other involves behavior seen outwardly, such as hyperactivity, inattention, and conduct problems.

The main pattern was this: a more conflictual relationship was linked with more screen time at a later point. More screen time was then linked with both types of behavior problems. Conflict was also directly linked with those problems.

In the study’s statistical model, screen time accounted for part of the connection between conflict and later behavior problems. It did not account for the whole connection.

A closer parent-child relationship was linked with fewer behavior problems. However, closeness did not show a significant path to later screen time.

record.canonical_text:
A bench does not move. But it can help a person keep moving.

For an older adult, a long walk can become several shorter steps. There is time to stop, sit, and rest before walking again.

A study in three neighboring areas of Vancouver listened to adults aged 60 and older. Researchers used seated interviews and walk-along talks. They met 28 participants in 2012 and 22 in 2014.

The older adults said benches helped them enjoy green spaces and places by the water. The seats gave them rest during walks. They also supported short talks and a feeling of connection.

The researchers described this with a warm image:

“Benches become like porches.”

A porch is between private life and public life. A neighborhood bench can play a similar role.

A 2023 review gives a wider view. It studied 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. The review reported that older park users preferred more benches, linked to their wish to relax.

record.canonical_text:
A public bench is easy to ignore—until you need one.

For older adults, a place to sit can shape how they experience a neighborhood. A study in three nearby Vancouver neighborhoods interviewed adults aged 60 and older. They said benches gave them places to rest during walks. Benches also helped them enjoy green areas and waterfront spaces.

But the role of a bench did not end there.

The study described how benches can “become like porches.” They are neither fully private nor fully social. They create a simple place where neighbors can stop, talk, or just spend time near one another.

A 2023 review added a wider view. It examined 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. The review reported that older park users preferred more benches, linked to their desire to relax. Other literature in the review said that well-kept parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets, and cafés encouraged older visitors.

record.canonical_text:
At the same time, some public benches have been changed to limit how people use them.

Sloped seats and center armrests can prevent people from lying across a bench. In other cases, benches are removed completely. These choices are often discussed as “hostile architecture” or “defensive architecture.”

This creates a difficult question:

Is a bench only a seat—or is it part of someone’s ability to move through the city?

A design that blocks one activity may also remove a resting place for someone else. Yet the evidence about the wider harm remains limited. As of March 2020, one article reported that no wide-scale empirical study had measured the effects of hostile architecture on homeless people or other targeted groups.

Yet officials said it was steeper than ordered and later corrected. In 2021, an NYC Transit post linked bench removals to homeless people sleeping. It was deleted, and the MTA called it an error—not a confirmed policy.

But benches are not always treated as invitations. Some cities have used defensive, or hostile, design. This can mean sloped seats, center armrests, or removing benches. These changes may make it harder to sleep or lie down.

So one small object now sits inside a larger city question:

“Is public space only for moving through, or is it also for stopping and staying?”

record.canonical_text:
A public bench looks like a small piece of street furniture. But for an older person, it can help turn a difficult journey into a possible one.

It offers a place to rest, enjoy a park or waterfront, and stay close to neighborhood life.

A 2016 qualitative study in Vancouver reported these experiences among adults aged 60 and older. Benches were not only seats. They could also be informal meeting places, where casual contact happened without a plan.

A 2023 review examined 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. It looked at how public parks can support active aging and well-being. Older park users preferred more benches and associated them with relaxation. Well-maintained parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets, and cafés were also reported to encourage older visitors.

A public bench looks like a small piece of street furniture. But for an older person, it can help turn a difficult journey into a possible one.

It offers a place to rest, enjoy a park or waterfront, and stay close to neighborhood life.

A 2016 qualitative study in Vancouver reported these experiences among adults aged 60 and older. Benches were not only seats. They could also be informal meeting places, where casual contact happened without a plan.

A 2023 review examined 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. It looked at how public parks can support active aging and well-being. Older park users preferred more benches and associated them with relaxation. Well-maintained parks with seating, pleasant paths, toilets, and cafés were also reported to encourage older visitors.

record.canonical_text:
Imagine you are reading, studying, or working.

Your phone is on the desk. You do not touch it. You do not even look at the screen.

Then comes a short notification sound.

You keep your eyes on your work. But your attention may already have moved.

A study published in 2022 tested this idea with 73 university students. They completed a simple visual task many times. Some rounds included a phone notification sound. Other rounds included a neutral sound.

The students did not look at or touch a phone during the task.

Even so, they answered more slowly after hearing the notification sound. A brain-wave signal was also larger. The researchers understood this as a sign that the students needed extra mental effort to keep working.

record.canonical_text:
A supermarket is not just a place where products wait for shoppers. It is also a carefully planned map.

That map often changes. A 2025 trade article says stores regularly update their layouts to make the shop feel fresh, guide customer movement, highlight seasonal offers, and encourage impulse buying.

But a new layout can also support healthier shopping.

In a 2021 study published in *PLoS Medicine*, Vogel and colleagues followed six discount supermarkets in the UK. Three stores changed their layout, while three similar stores acted as comparison stores.

The changes were practical. The fruit and vegetable area became larger and moved closer to the entrance. Frozen vegetables were moved to a more visible aisle. Sweets were removed from displays near the checkouts and replaced with non-food items and water.

record.canonical_text:
The results showed a clear change in the sales mix. After three months, fruit and vegetable sales rose by 1.71 standard deviations, equal to about 6,170 portions per store each week. After six months, the increase reached 2.42 standard deviations, or about 9,820 portions per store each week.

Snack sales fell by 1.05 standard deviations after three months. That was about 1,359 fewer portions per store each week. At six months, snack sales were still lower, but the result was not statistically significant.

There was also an important limit. Total sales for the whole store did not change significantly. The new layout appeared to change what people bought, rather than how much the store sold overall.

A related survey of 150 women found that fruit and vegetable purchases increased in households using the intervention stores, while they decreased in comparison households. However, the study did not find a significant effect on snack purchases.

record.canonical_text:
A café is no longer only a place for coffee and conversation.

For some people, it is also a place to work. They buy a drink, open a laptop, and stay for many hours. Researchers call these people customer-workers: customers who also work in the café.

A 2021 study looked at this change in London. The researchers studied 38 third places. They made 52 visits, interviewed 27 customers and 12 service providers, and also looked at 55 media sources.

The study found four kinds of third place.

Archetypal places try to stop people from working. They may not offer Wi-Fi. They may play loud music or use less comfortable chairs.

Status Quo places do not clearly choose between workers and social customers. Because of this, clashes between the two groups can be strong.

Compromise places try to welcome both groups. But they can have trouble making their rules work every day.

record.canonical_text:
A café is no longer only a place for coffee and conversation. For some people, it is also a place to work for hours with a laptop. These “customer-workers” buy something, take a seat, and use a public space for work-related tasks.

For café owners, this creates a difficult choice. Should they welcome this customer group, or protect the space for shorter visits and social use? Two recent sources show that both answers are now being tested.

A 2021 qualitative study by L. Mimoun and A. Gruen, published in the *Journal of Service Research*, examined this question. In London, it covered 38 third places. Researchers made 52 observation visits, interviewed 27 customers and 12 service providers, and reviewed 55 media sources.

The study places these businesses into four groups. Archetypal places discourage work. Status Quo places do not clearly choose between workers and social customers, and this is where conflict is described as strongest. Compromise places try to serve both groups but may struggle to enforce their rules. Productive Third Places, or PTPs, clearly target customer-workers and adapt the space for them.

A café is no longer only a place for coffee and conversation. For some people, it is also a place to work for hours with a laptop. These “customer-workers” buy something, take a seat, and use a public space for work-related tasks.

For café owners, this creates a difficult choice. Should they welcome this customer group, or protect the space for shorter visits and social use? Two recent sources show that both answers are now being tested.

The other response is restriction. In a report published by *Coffee Intelligence* on April twenty eighth, 2026, The Barn introduced a one-hour laptop limit, or a full laptop ban on certain busy days. At its Neukölln store in Berlin, the café reported that laptop users occupied more than 70 percent of seats for long periods. It also reported a 25 percent loss in sales before the policy change.

The Barn’s founder, Ralf Rüller, said the business wants to offer an excellent coffee experience. At the same time, he recognizes the demand from remote workers who want to work in cafés.

So the debate is not simply about laptops. It is about whether a café treats work as a problem, a compromise, or a planned part of its identity.

So we open the tracking page. Then, a few minutes later, we check it again. Nothing may have changed. Still, the update button pulls us back.

What looks like simple impatience may be part of a wider response to uncertain waiting.

A 2025 longitudinal study by Howell and Sweeny, published in *Emotion*, followed three groups over periods ranging from several weeks to several months. They included voters waiting for the 2020 United States presidential election result, people waiting for their California bar exam results, and academic job applicants waiting for hiring decisions.

The pattern was clear: as people became more worried, they searched more often for news and updates.

record.canonical_text:
Other passengers can make the line grow. When one person stands, nearby people may stand too. The gate becomes a place where people watch each other and follow the crowd.

American Airlines has begun using new technology at one airport to manage this problem.

American Airlines opened nine gates at Dallas Fort Worth on June 8, 2026. All nine have electronic boarding gate technology.

The system checks each boarding pass automatically before the gate opens. It is designed to control the speed of boarding and reduce the need for gate workers to stop passengers trying to board too early.

American Airlines announced the plan earlier this year. The company says it may bring the technology to more hub and gateway airports in the future.

record.canonical_text:
At an airport gate, a line can start before anyone asks for one. The passenger’s boarding group has not been called, yet people gather near the gate and prepare to board. Flight attendants have a name for this behavior: “gate lice.”

The behavior may look wasteful. But psychologists do not describe it as simply irrational.

Psychologist Stephen Reicher explains it as a response to uneven risks. If a passenger delays joining the line, there may be a small chance of missing a connecting flight. If they stand early, the cost is much smaller: a few unnecessary minutes of waiting.

That calculation can turn a quiet gate area into a crowded one. Standing in line feels like a way to stay ready, even when the boarding group has not been called.

record.canonical_text:
But this logic has a clear limit.

Growth is not magic. If each new customer does not make the product stronger, fast spending may only make a weak business larger. Easy money can also hide problems and reduce the pressure to become efficient.

NFX therefore suggests changing the goal as a startup grows. Once people clearly want the product, a Seed or Series A company may aim to grow three to five times in one year. At Series B or C, growth should come with efficient ways to get customers. Later, the company should move toward profit.

In 2020, Kuratko, Holt, and Neubert also examined blitzscaling in the peer-reviewed journal *Business Horizons*. Blitzscaling means choosing very fast growth over efficiency. The real question is not simply, “Can we grow fast?” It is, “Does speed create a lasting advantage?”

record.canonical_text:
For some startups, profit is not the first finish line.

They spend heavily to gain users, enter markets, and grow faster than competitors. This can look dangerous. But when a company has a real network effect, speed may have a clear economic purpose.

Research by Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro in 1985 explained the basic idea. A product may become more valuable to each user as more people use it.

That can start a powerful cycle.

More users create more value. More value attracts more users. An early lead may then build into a lasting advantage. In these markets, even the product with the best technology does not always win. Starting late can become a growing problem.

record.canonical_text:
Pete Flint of NFX argued in 2020 that companies with genuine network effects may have good reasons to choose growth before profit. Some markets can become “winner-take-most” races. After reaching critical mass, a company may also have a chance to move from losses to profit.

But there is a trap hidden inside the word “growth.”

A rising customer count does not prove that a strong network is forming. NFX presents Groupon as a warning. Its fast expansion hid the loss of merchants and sellers that could not be sustained.

The article also points to some direct-to-consumer companies in mattresses, shoes, and meal kits. They used blitzscaling-style growth without strong network effects or other clear defenses. Several later faced lower-value funding rounds and investor losses.

In other words, speed can build a fortress—or simply make a weak business burn money faster.

A towel can come out of the wash looking clean, then give off a wet-cloth or old-rag smell. That smell may be noticed before washing, while the fabric is still wet after washing, or after the laundry has dried, and these stages can overlap.

A 2022 survey asked 359 households about laundry odors. About 110 reported a smell before washing, while fewer noticed one in wet laundry after washing or after the laundry had dried. These groups could overlap, so the numbers are not a rate for all households. But they show that the wash cycle does not always mark the end of the story.

As of September 2026, the factory AI story has two clocks.

Investment plans are moving fast. But broad use inside factories is moving more slowly.

Worldwide, factories installed 542,000 industrial robots in 2024. That was more than twice the number from ten years earlier. The robotics industry says AI and machines that can do more by themselves are the top robotics trend for 2026.

Business plans point in the same direction. In a survey of manufacturing leaders, 80 percent said they plan to put at least 20 percent of their improvement budget into software, sensors, and other tools for smarter factories.

record.canonical_text:
By September 2026, the manufacturing world is sending two messages at once.

The first is clear: interest in AI and robots is rising quickly. Global industrial robot installations have more than doubled in ten years. A robotics group now lists AI and self-directed robots as the top robotics trend for 2026.

Business plans tell a similar story. In one survey, 80 percent of manufacturing leaders said they plan to put at least 20 percent of their improvement budget into smart manufacturing tools. These tools include automation equipment, sensors, data systems, and AI that can make some decisions on its own.

But plans are moving faster than working systems.

record.canonical_text:
At the same time, silence can also bring calm. In one study of roughly 46 students, six minutes and 30 seconds of silence increased relaxation in both a university room and a city garden. The outdoor setting also brought less boredom and a stronger feeling of being in the present moment.

Research on the body shows the same mixed picture. A review of 37 studies found that responses to silence depend on the kind of silence, the setting, familiarity, surrounding noise, and other personal factors. In a study that measured heart activity, one noise condition showed more activity linked with the body’s calming system than silence, while white noise showed more activity linked with its alerting system than that noise.

People also differ across studies and cultures. In a study of about 2,500 college students in 11 countries, an everyday activity was enjoyed more than thinking for pleasure. This was true in every country tested. Still, differences between countries were linked with personal factors such as openness, meditation experience, starting mood, and phone use. In one Japan–United States survey, Japanese respondents viewed silence more negatively with strangers than with close friends, while Americans did not show that difference.

record.canonical_text:
The scale is real in some places, but the timeline is uneven. Amazon reports 600 million active Alexa endpoints across devices, cars, offices, Fire TV, and Prime Video. “Active endpoints” is Amazon’s term, not a count of unique people. Amazon also reports that customers talked to Alexa twice as much and completed purchases on devices three times more often. Music streaming and smart-home use also rose. The company does not state the comparison period in the cited letter.

Tens of millions joined Alexa+ Early Access before it became available to all U.S. customers. The company says millions of Ray-Ban Meta glasses have sold. But Google’s Android XR products are at different stages: the Galaxy XR headset is already available, audio-only glasses are planned for fall 2026, and the camera glasses with an optional lens display have no separate confirmed launch date in the cited evidence.

That mix points to gradual layering, not one sudden replacement.

record.canonical_text:
The safety reports draw a line here. A 2025 international report said existing systems were not able to undermine human control in a meaningful way at the time of that report. A later report describes a severe loss-of-control scenario as requiring three things together: enough ability, a harmful tendency to use it, and a setting that gives the system access and opportunity. It says experts do not agree on the exact mix.

Warnings about the future should be labeled as warnings. Experts disagree about how likely and how severe such scenarios may be. One company called an assessed risk “very low, but not completely negligible.” The evidence summarized here does not establish claims about superintelligence, an intelligence explosion, or the singularity.

So the current picture is neither “nothing is happening” nor “AI is already in charge.” Capability growth is measured. Boundary failures have been observed in special conditions. Human monitoring and intervention can work in some cases, but they are not perfect or universal.

record.canonical_text:
Space security news often uses one phrase for very different things: weapons in space.

That phrase came into focus on September 14, 2026. U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States was deploying orbital “space control weapons” to protect U.S. forces from hostile actions. An official U.S. Space Force article called this the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had deployed weapons in space.

But the statement did not name the systems or explain how they could attack another satellite. No target was identified.

The wider term is “counterspace.” A 2025 U.S. Space Force framework uses that term for actions in orbit, through communication links, and on the ground. It can include physical attacks, electronic interference, and cyber operations.

record.canonical_text: The legal picture is narrower than the technology picture. The Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, and prohibits installing such weapons on the Moon and other celestial bodies. It also requires space activity to follow international law. But it does not completely ban every conventional anti-satellite missile, jammer, or cyber operation. United Nations votes in 2024 and 2025 supported existing principles and further arms-control work, but they did not create a new comprehensive treaty. The U.S. pledge against destructive direct-ascent tests remains a national policy commitment.

record.canonical_text:
Fashion keeps asking a small question: are mini and micro bags returning?

The evidence says they are visible again. But they are not simply replacing larger bags.

In Spring/Summer 2025, one fashion report said scaled-down minis were being pushed aside by capacious totes and practical doctor-bag shapes. Its Fall/Winter 2025 roundup made a similar point. Most of the handbags shown were roomy enough for everyday use.

That makes a broad, straight-line comeback difficult to support.

Why bring a human into an AI phone call? Because some people hung up after realizing they were speaking with an AI. Muse could say the words, but the other person might refuse to stay for the conversation. The machine had learned an awkward lesson: sounding human is not the same as being welcomed as a caller.

In some internal tests, calls handled by humans had a reported success rate of 95% to 98%. Reuters said AI-only calls performed worse, but did not provide an exact number. So the experiment became more than a test of speech technology. It became a test of trust, with Muse giving instructions backstage while a human took the stage.

You go to buy your usual coffee, then stop. “Hey, when did you go upscale?” The first thing that comes to mind is tariffs. You want to say, “So you’re the culprit!” But a great detective takes a breath here. Let’s turn back the clock on this case.

In the United States, the average price of ground coffee rose 41% from the same month a year earlier, according to reports based on government figures. This is about ground coffee, not a cup at a café. Before you buy something to wake you up, the price shocks your wallet awake.

But according to Reuters, most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages that began before the summer tariffs and from higher prices for the beans themselves. Wait a minute. The case had started before the suspect we had our eye on even appeared.

The investigation leads us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. People had also stopped hoping that the next harvest would be better. “Will there be enough beans?” Before we think about how to brew them, we must ask if there will be any beans to brew at all.

We turn the pages of the record and find this. In February, before summer, New York’s Arabica coffee futures price reached a record high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores. It was the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded.

“So, were tariffs not to blame?” No. That would be deciding too soon, too. Reuters also reported that U.S. tariffs put in place during summer raised the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must put events in the right order.

“Coffee prices are falling!” Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, “News? I haven’t heard any.” If bean prices have fallen, why don’t we pay less?

First, let’s go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down.

At about the same time, ICE’s future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, “coffee price,” but they mean different things.

At about the same time, ICE futures prices for Arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

record.canonical_text:
US roasters keep green beans in stock. Then they roast and pack them. Reports also say price talks with stores often happen every three months. There are several steps between the beans and the store shelf. Even when market prices fall, not every step responds, “Got it, cut prices now!”

Of course, around nine months is an estimate from market experts and others. It is not a timer for every company. It is not a promise that prices will definitely be lower nine months from now. It is too soon to circle a sale on your calendar.

In other words, a fall in market prices is not an update button for price tags. The prices on shelves may reflect purchases and talks from some time ago. Next time you see a headline about falling prices, ask the price tag. Say, “By the way, how many months ago did you get here?”

record.canonical_text:
“Beans have gotten cheaper!” At that news, your wallet pumps its fist. In your mind, the price of your usual cup has already come down, too. But the price tag in a shop may not change right away. When you see a price tag that makes you want to say, “Haven’t you heard the news?”, it seems there is a time lag.

The price measure reported by the International Coffee Organization fell 8.7% from the previous month. The reason, it said, was that more beans harvested in Brazil had entered the market, and a good supply was expected to continue.

The US Department of Agriculture said that earlier high prices came from several factors happening at once: bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam, fewer beans available for sale, and strong demand.

record.canonical_text:
This news feels like a short play in three acts. Act One was “20%.” Act Two brought an unexpected turn. Act Three was an unexpected move in oil prices.

The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe.

But “20%” was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay, how the money would be collected, or what legal basis would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage.

The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

About 24 hours and 48 minutes later, at 11:04 a.m. on July 14, Trump said the 20% plan would be replaced by trade and investment projects between Gulf states and the US. record.canonical_text:
Ring, ring. A call came from an AI agent—or so it seemed. As the conversation went on, the voice on the other end turned out not to be AI at all, but a person.

Meta had run a test that created exactly this kind of surprise.

The setting was the phone feature of its AI agent, Muse. In some calls made through Muse, trained contract workers, rather than AI, placed the calls and carried the conversations through to the end.

It was as if someone took off an AI costume and a person stepped out.

Having a person take over is not necessarily bad. A human can handle situations that AI alone finds difficult. As a system, that may even be useful.

But this is where the problem began. When a human staff member handled a call, sensitive information from the user could be shared with a contract worker at a call center.

There is a big difference between speaking because you think you are talking to a machine and speaking after you know a person is listening. When people share their names, plans, or personal circumstances, knowing who is on the other end matters.

record.canonical_text: Today's topic is “Can’t Wait for the Next Episode”? Make One Yourself? “byUs” Lets You Make Stories with Characters You Love.

record.canonical_text:
“Wait, it ends here!?” Have you ever shouted that when a manga ends at an exciting moment? It says the story will continue next time. What will that character say next? What will happen to the two of them? It may be a shame to keep those ideas only in your head.

The company that runs LINE Manga has announced a new service. It is called “byUs,” an AI chat service for stories. It is pronounced “bias.” You can talk with characters you love. You can also make your own stories based on their works. You can leave the reader’s seat and step onto the stage of making stories.

If you thought, “Can’t you already talk with characters?” you noticed something important. LINE Manga already has a service called “Character Chat.” The company says byUs lets you do more than chat. You can also make stories more freely. So, you can ask not only, “What should we talk about next?” but also, “What should happen next?”

record.canonical_text:
For example, you can continue an official story on the service. Or you can make your own story as a fan. “What if that person came here?” “If it were me, I’d want to see this happen.” The ideas that grew as you turned each page can now start your own stories. You may wait to see what happens next. Or you may use that time to think up what happens next.

You can also publish your fan stories, if you want to. You can keep them private, or let someone else read them. But things change when you make a story public. “Will people understand this story?” “I want to think a little more about what happens next.” Before you know it, you may think like a story-maker, though you began as a reader.

“Won’t attack.” When you hear those words, you may already be ending the meeting in your mind. You may think, “So Britain will only defend.” But wait! One important detail is missing from the meeting notes: who will not attack? This time, the news detective must find the subject.

First, let’s look at the announcement. A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said they had stopped and destroyed one ballistic missile. The Houthis had fired it toward Riyadh.

In this case, the UK Ministry of Defence announced an air-defense mission for Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets. They will protect Saudi cities and important sites from air attacks. Their mission is only to defend. The jets will not attack the Houthis.

This news feels like a short play in three acts. Act One was “20%.” Act Two brought a surprise. Act Three was an unexpected move in oil prices.

The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted about a US plan. The United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe.

But “20%” was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay. It did not say how the money would be collected. It did not say what law would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage.

The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

record.canonical_text: The hidden person behind the AI sign Here was the reveal. The test began without clearly telling users that contract workers would make the calls. A user might think the exchange was with AI, even though a person was involved. AI had not learned to speak like a human. A human stood behind the sign that said AI. It seemed like a story from the future. But the main question was very basic: Had users been clearly told who was making the call? As AI becomes able to make calls or reservations for us, this question will become more familiar. The more useful the feature, the more people will want to know who is on the other side. They will want to know if it is AI or human.

record.canonical_text: Ring, ring. A call came from an AI agent—or so it seemed. As the conversation went on, the voice on the other end turned out not to be AI at all, but a person. Meta had run a test that created exactly this kind of surprise. The setting was the phone feature of its AI agent, Muse. In some calls made through Muse, trained contract workers, rather than AI, placed the calls and carried the conversations through to the end. It was as if someone took off an AI costume and a person stepped out. Having a person take over is not necessarily bad. A human can handle situations that AI alone finds difficult. As a system, that may even be useful. But this is where the problem began. When a human staff member handled a call, sensitive information from the user could be shared with a contract worker at a call center. There is a big difference between speaking because you think you are talking to a machine and speaking after you know a person is listening. When people share their names, plans, or personal circumstances, knowing who is on the other end matters.

record.canonical_text: This news feels like a short play in 3 acts. Act One was 20%. Act 2 brought an unexpected turn. Act 3 was an unexpected move in oil prices. The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe. But 20% was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay, how the money would be collected, or what legal basis would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

record.canonical_text:
This news feels like a short play in three acts. Act One was “20%.” Act Two brought an unexpected turn. Act Three was an unexpected move in oil prices.

The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe.

But “20%” was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay, how the money would be collected, or what legal basis would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage.

The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted about a US plan. The United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe. But 20% was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay. It did not say how the money would be collected. It did not say what law would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

record.canonical_text: The problem was not that humans made the calls. The problem was how users were told who was speaking. People who asked Muse to make a call might think AI was doing it. But sometimes, a human was speaking instead. If this was not explained clearly, users could not know if it was AI or a person. They enjoyed the ease of AI. But they did not know that a human was on the other end. This was happening behind the scenes. Also, a call might need user information to continue. That information might then be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised this inside the company as a privacy concern.

record.canonical_text: Coffee prices are falling! Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, News? I haven't heard any. If bean prices have fallen, why don't we pay less? First, let's go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down. At about the same time, ICE's future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

record.canonical_text: US roasters keep green beans in stock. Then they roast and pack them. Reports also say price talks with stores often happen every 3 months. There are several steps between the beans and the store shelf. Even when market prices fall, not every step responds, Got it, cut prices now! Of course, around 9 months is an estimate from market experts and others. It is not a timer for every company. It is not a promise that prices will definitely be lower 9 months from now. It is too soon to circle a sale on your calendar. In other words, a fall in market prices is not an update button for price tags. The prices on shelves may reflect purchases and talks from some time ago. Next time you see a headline about falling prices, ask the price tag. Say, By the way, how many months ago did you get here?

A shop's price tag does not change the moment the market moves.

record.canonical_text: Coffee prices are falling! Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, News? I haven't heard any. If bean prices have fallen, why don't we pay less? First, let's go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down. At about the same time, ICE's future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

record.canonical_text: This news feels like a short play in 3 acts. Act One was 20%. Act 2 brought a surprise. Act 3 was an unexpected move in oil prices. The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted about a US plan. The United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe. But 20% was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay. It did not say how the money would be collected. It did not say what law would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

record.canonical_text: The problem was not that humans made the calls. The problem was how users were told who was speaking. People who asked Muse to make a call might think AI was doing it. But sometimes, a human was speaking instead. If this was not explained clearly, users could not know if it was AI or a person. They enjoyed the ease of AI. But they did not know that a human was on the other end. This was happening behind the scenes. Also, a call might need user information to continue. That information might then be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised this inside the company as a privacy concern.

record.canonical_text: Coffee prices are falling! Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, News? I haven't heard any. If bean prices have fallen, why don't we pay less? First, let's go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down. At about the same time, ICE's future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

record.canonical_text: US roasters keep green beans in stock. Then they roast and pack them. Reports also say price talks with stores often happen every 3 months. There are several steps between the beans and the store shelf. Even when market prices fall, not every step responds, Got it, cut prices now! Of course, around 9 months is an estimate from market experts and others. It is not a timer for every company. It is not a promise that prices will definitely be lower 9 months from now. It is too soon to circle a sale on your calendar. In other words, a fall in market prices is not an update button for price tags. The prices on shelves may reflect purchases and talks from some time ago. Next time you see a headline about falling prices, ask the price tag. Say, By the way, how many months ago did you get here?

He said the 20% plan would be replaced by trade and investment projects between Gulf states and the US. He cited very productive discussions with Middle Eastern leaders. He also said no one should charge ships in the Strait. He said he disliked fees. The change was sudden. But the dates must stay separate to understand the oil move. On July 13, Brent rose 9.59% and settled at $83.30. Reuters linked that rise to concern about a US sea blockade of Iran. The blockade was planned for the next day. Reuters also linked it to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

record.canonical_text: Vogue also covered the 2026 season. It showed small pouches from Prada and Loewe. It also showed Celine's Ultra Maxi and Altuzarra's large shoulder bag. It showed roomy totes from Toteme and other brands, too. This list matters. Large bags had not disappeared. Small and large bags appeared in the same season. We are not seeing mini bags spread through the whole market. Instead, they are back in fashion reports and on certain runways. Even so, trends now look different. Bags no longer play a game with only one size on the throne. Large bags are the luggage crew. They carry what we need. Mini bags are the stage crew. They catch the eye and set the mood. In 2026, the runway proudly shows this split in their work.

record.canonical_text: Coffee prices are falling! Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, News? I haven't heard any. If bean prices have fallen, why don't we pay less? First, let's go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down. At about the same time, ICE's future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

record.canonical_text: After that, an index showing world market prices fell by 25% over 7 months. The USDA links this drop to extra supplies becoming easier to get. But in the United States, the coffee part of the Consumer Price Index was still higher than in the same month a year earlier. Wait a minute, that doesn't add up! You might want to say that. But one is a world market index, and the other is the US Consumer Price Index. One shows a drop over 7 months, while the other compares prices with a year earlier. They are on different stages and run on different clocks. If you pour the numbers into the same cup, the story gets muddled. And price tags follow their own schedule. Market experts and others interviewed by Reuters estimated that it takes around 9 months or longer for green-bean prices to show up in store prices. If market prices are a breaking news alert, price tags are patient letters.

For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

But 20% was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay, how the money would be collected, or what legal basis would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

record.canonical_text: Beyond the river, attackers blocked the road. One grabbed his arm. Another swung a stick. Melos struck out, broke free, and stumbled past them. Their angry shouts followed him, but he did not look back. By afternoon, pain filled every step. Then his legs gave way. He lay with his face against the earth. The city was still far away. He could not reach it. He could not even stand. He could stay here. No one would find him before sunset. His friend would die, but he would live. For one terrible moment, the thought brought relief. Then he remembered those warm fingers around his hand.

record.canonical_text: Coffee prices are falling! Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, News? I haven't heard any. If bean prices have fallen, why don't we pay less? First, let's go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down. At about the same time, ICE's future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

record.canonical_text: The office is making room for an old idea: a desk that belongs to you. In some workplaces, assigned desks are returning. Companies are reducing their reliance on hot-desking, a system in which workers are not given a personal desk and use whichever desk is free. Scotiabank and iCapital Network are among the companies connected to this quiet shift, according to reporting from Bisnow's New York Office Conference. The change comes as employees express dissatisfaction with hot-desking. Korn Ferry points to several concerns. The office may compare poorly with a home workspace. Workers may sit close to unfamiliar colleagues. The daily work setting may also feel less predictable and less consistent.

record.canonical_text: One reason the desk matters may be psychological, not practical. In Gensler data reported by Bisnow, 87% of workers with assigned desks reported a sense of belonging at work, compared with 74% of workers without assigned desks. record.canonical_text: ## Main Story Walk into some offices today, and one old idea is quietly returning: the assigned desk. An assigned desk is kept for one worker. It is different from hot-desking. In a hot-desking office, workers do not have a fixed desk. They choose an empty desk when they arrive. Hot-desking became more common than before the pandemic. It allowed companies to use desks as shared space. But some workers have not been happy with the system. They want a work area that feels more stable and predictable.

record.canonical_text: The result was clear for fruit and vegetables. After 3 months, sales rose by 1.71 standard deviations. In everyday terms, that was about 6,170 portions more per store each week. After 6 months, the increase was 2.42 standard deviations, or about 9,820 more portions each week. Sweets moved in the other direction. After 3 months, sales fell by 1.05 standard deviations. That was about 1,359 fewer portions per store each week. However, total store sales did not change in a statistically significant way. A related survey included 150 women aged 18 to 45. Fruit and vegetable buying increased in households using the changed stores, while it fell in comparison households. Sweets buying did not show a significant effect.

record.canonical_text: A café is no longer only a place for coffee and conversation. For some people, it is also a place to work for hours with a laptop. These customer-workers buy something, take a seat, and use a public space for work-related tasks. For café owners, this creates a difficult choice. Should they welcome this customer group, or protect the space for shorter visits and social use? 2 recent sources show that both answers are now being tested. A 2021 qualitative study by L. Mimoun and A. Gruen, published in the *Journal of Service Research*, examined this question. In London, it covered 38 third places. Researchers made 52 observation visits, interviewed 27 customers and 12 service providers, and reviewed 55 media sources. The study places these businesses into 4 groups. Archetypal places discourage work. Status Quo places do not clearly choose between workers and social customers, and this is where conflict is described as strongest. Compromise places try to serve both groups but may struggle to enforce their rules. Productive Third Places, or PTPs, clearly target customer-workers and adapt the space for them.

record.canonical_text: At an airport gate, a line can start before anyone asks for one. The passenger's boarding group has not been called, yet people gather near the gate and prepare to board. Flight attendants have a name for this behavior: gate lice. The behavior may look wasteful. But psychologists do not describe it as simply irrational. Psychologist Stephen Reicher explains it as a response to uneven risks. If a passenger delays joining the line, there may be a small chance of missing a connecting flight. If they stand early, the cost is much smaller: a few unnecessary minutes of waiting. That calculation can turn a quiet gate area into a crowded one. Standing in line feels like a way to stay ready, even when the boarding group has not been called.

record.canonical_text: ## Main Story At a café or restaurant, the bill may end with a question: how much would you like to tip? A screen often shows a few suggested percentages and asks you to pick one. The word recommended sounds helpful. But it can also become the first number in your mind. Before you decide what the service was worth, the screen may have already set a starting point. A 2014 study looked closely at this idea using more than 13 million credit card transactions in New York City taxis. Around a $15 fare, the recommended tip menu changed suddenly. The researchers used this change in a regression discontinuity design.

record.canonical_text: A phone does not need to light up in your hand to change a task. A sound may be enough. In another study, even a silent phone on a desk was linked to lower attention. A study by Upshaw, Stevens, Ganis, and Zabelina tested 73 college students. They worked through a letter task for 960 trials. In some trials, they heard a notification sound. In others, they heard a neutral sound. They did not look at or touch a phone. The result was clear: responses were slower during trials with notification sounds. Brain recordings also showed a larger signal after those sounds. This happened even though the students kept working and did not check a screen.

record.canonical_text: A second study by Skowronek, Seifert, and Lindberg tested 42 university students. Their phones were powered off, and no notifications arrived. The researchers compared a phone on the desk with a phone in another room. Performance was lower when the phone stayed on the desk. The attention score averaged about 100 on the desk, compared with about 109 when the phone was away. Processing speed showed the same pattern: it was lower when the phone stayed on the desk. Together, these studies show 2 different moments. A notification can affect a person during a task. A phone can also be linked to lower performance without making a sound.

record.canonical_text: The most important question in the new space-security story is not simply whether satellites can be attacked. It is this: Is the weapon itself in orbit? On September 14, 2026, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit. He said they were meant to protect U.S. forces from hostile actions. An official U.S. Space Force article published the next day described this as the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had put weapons in orbit.

record.canonical_text: Space security news often uses one phrase for very different things: weapons in space. That phrase came into focus on September 14, 2026. U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States was deploying orbital space control weapons to protect U.S. forces from hostile actions. An official U.S. Space Force article called this the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had deployed weapons in space. But the statement did not name the systems or explain how they could attack another satellite. No target was identified. The wider term is counterspace. A 2025 U.S. Space Force framework uses that term for actions in orbit, through communication links, and on the ground. It can include physical attacks, electronic interference, and cyber operations.

record.canonical_text: The same pattern appeared in 2026. Small pouches appeared at Prada, Loewe, Miu Miu, and Valentino. At the same time, very large bags appeared at Celine, Altuzarra, Toteme, Stella McCartney, and Kallmeyer. Some Fall/Winter 2026 shoulder bags from Chanel, Miu Miu, and Bottega Veneta were even large enough for a laptop. Mini bags also received strong attention from fashion editors. One fashion magazine called them a major Fall 2026 styling direction. But another offered a more mixed view, saying that autumn was bringing back larger bags while still keeping smaller clutches and top-handle bags in the picture. One trend company also reported a 152% rise in retail adoption for oversized clutches in 2026. That is a company estimate, but it adds an important counterpoint. The clearest answer is this: tiny bags are gaining attention in some fashion spaces, but they are not winning everywhere. Small and large bags are appearing side by side.

record.canonical_text: ## Main Story A lemon tart with chopped pickles sounds like a joke—or at least a strange snack. But Lawson says an AI program suggested the pairing, and it became the starting point for a real convenience-store product. The idea did not stay on a computer screen. Human product specialists made samples, tasted them, and adjusted the taste and appearance. Lawson then planned a sale of the finished product.

record.canonical_text: This news feels like a short play in 3 acts. Act One was 20%. Act 2 brought a surprise. Act 3 was an unexpected move in oil prices. The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted about a US plan. The United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe. But 20% was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay. It did not say how the money would be collected. It did not say what law would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

record.canonical_text: At the same time, US data on what people pay showed coffee cost 6.1% more than in the same month a year earlier. You might wonder, Did prices fall or rise? But this data was for a different month than the bean price measure. It also does not show the price of coffee at a cafe. Don't put the 2 numbers in the ring just yet. So, how long does it take for bean prices to reach a price tag? People in the market and experts spoke with Reuters. They estimate raw-bean prices take at least about 9 months to appear in US shop prices. The road to a price tag is quite a long journey. The article says US companies that roast coffee keep raw beans in stock. Roasting and packing the beans also take time. These companies often talk with stores about prices on a regular basis. A shop's price tag does not change the moment the market moves.

record.canonical_text: The investigation leads us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. People had also stopped hoping that the next harvest would be better. Will there be enough beans? Before we think about how to brew them, we must ask if there will be any beans to brew at all. We turn the pages of the record and find this. In February, before summer, New York's Arabica coffee futures price reached a record high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores. It was the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded. So, were tariffs not to blame? No. That would be deciding too soon, too. Reuters also reported that U.S. tariffs put in place during summer raised the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must put events in the right order.

record.canonical_text: Today's topic is Can't Wait for the Next Episode? Make One Yourself? byUs Lets You Make Stories with Characters You Love.
record.primary_text: Today's topic is, can't wait for the next episode? Make one yourself? Buy us lets you make stories with characters you love.
record.secondary_text: Today's topic is, can't wait for the next episode? Make one yourself? Buy us lets you make stories with characters you love.

record.canonical_text: Wait, it ends here!? Have you ever shouted that when a manga ends at an exciting moment? It says the story will continue next time. What will that character say next? What will happen to the 2 of them? It may be a shame to keep those ideas only in your head. The company that runs LINE Manga has announced a new service. It is called byUs, an AI chat service for stories. It is pronounced bias. You can talk with characters you love. You can also make your own stories based on their works. You can leave the reader's seat and step onto the stage of making stories. If you thought, Can't you already talk with characters? you noticed something important. LINE Manga already has a service called Character Chat. The company says byUs lets you do more than chat. You can also make stories more freely. So, you can ask not only, What should we talk about next? but also, What should happen next?

record.canonical_text: For example, you can continue an official story on the service. Or you can make your own story as a fan. What if that person came here? If it were me, I'd want to see this happen. The ideas that grew as you turned each page can now start your own stories. You may wait to see what happens next. Or you may use that time to think up what happens next. You can also publish your fan stories, if you want to. You can keep them private, or let someone else read them. But things change when you make a story public. Will people understand this story? I want to think a little more about what happens next. Before you know it, you may think like a story-maker, though you began as a reader.

record.canonical_text: Of course, you cannot use just anything you like. Only works and characters approved by their original creators are allowed. The Help page also says the service has permission to use the original works it features. It has this permission through official agreements with their creators. This is the base that lets you enjoy asking, What if? The service first offered 2 works and 4 characters in Japan. Here, taking part in a story means moving the story forward through conversations. It also means making a story as a fan. Reading a work is fun. Now, it is also fun to think up what happens next. Until now, you could only say, If it were me, I'd do it this way, to yourself. With byUs, those words can help you start making a story. What will you say to a character you love? What will happen next in the story? So, where will your next part begin?

record.canonical_text: Wait, it ends here!? Have you ever blurted that out when a manga ends at an exciting moment and says the story will continue next time? What will that character say next? What will happen to the 2 of them? It might be a shame to let those ideas stay only in your head. The company that runs LINE Manga has announced the launch of byUs, an AI story chat service. It is pronounced bias. You can enjoy talking with your favorite characters and make your own stories based on the works. You can take a step from the reader's seat onto the stage of story-making. If you thought, Can't you already talk with characters? you've noticed something important. LINE Manga already has Character Chat. The company says the difference is that, as well as having conversations, you can make stories more freely. In other words, you can enjoy not only asking, What should we talk about next? but also, What should happen next?

record.canonical_text: For example, you can continue an official story in the service. Or you can make your own story as a fan. What if that person showed up here? If it were me, I'd want to see this happen. The ideas that grew with every turn of the page can now become a starting point for your own stories. The time spent waiting for what happens next may become time spent thinking up what happens next. What's more, you can publish the fan stories you make if you want to. You can enjoy them privately, or let someone else read them. But things change when you make a story public. Will people understand this plot? I want to work on what happens next a little more. You may find yourself thinking like a story-maker before you know it, even though you started out as a reader.

What will happen next in the story? So, where will your next part begin?

Not, “What’s different between me and that person who earns a lot?”
But, “How are my past self and my later self different?”

In a way, the researchers stopped comparing people with others. Instead, they followed each person over time. It is like putting down binoculars you use to look at your neighbor’s greener grass. Then you turn the pages of your own records.

Then came “diligence.” This means taking things seriously and working hard. When a person’s income went up, their diligence tended to rise later too. This link was small. The link also went the other way. When diligence rose, income tended to rise later. That link was small too.

It was not a link in only one direction. It went both ways. But this is important, so let me say it clearly: the links were “small.”

“So, earning more makes me more serious!”
Wait before you jump to that conclusion.

record.canonical_text:
“Wait, it ends here!?” Have you ever blurted that out when a manga ends at an exciting moment and says the story will continue next time? What will that character say next? What will happen to the two of them? It might be a shame to let those ideas stay only in your head.

The company that runs LINE Manga has announced the launch of “byUs,” an AI story chat service. It is pronounced “bias.” You can enjoy talking with your favorite characters and make your own stories based on the works. You can take a step from the reader’s seat onto the stage of story-making.

If you thought, “Can’t you already talk with characters?” you’ve noticed something important. LINE Manga already has “Character Chat.” The company says the difference is that, as well as having conversations, you can make stories more freely. In other words, you can enjoy not only asking, “What should we talk about next?” but also, “What should happen next?”

“Won’t attack.” When you hear those words, you may already be ending the meeting in your mind. You may think, “So Britain will only defend.” But wait! One important detail is missing from the meeting notes: who will not attack? This time, the news detective must find the subject.

First, let’s look at the announcement. A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said they had stopped and destroyed one ballistic missile. The Houthis had fired it toward Riyadh.

In this case, the UK Ministry of Defence announced an air-defense mission for Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets. They will protect Saudi cities and important sites from air attacks. Their mission is only to defend. The jets will not attack the Houthis.
